System design

Solar panels first, or battery first?

The order of investment changes the economics. Here is how to reason about it using your own bill.

Published 2 September 2026Updated 15 October 20267 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

A battery without solar has nothing to store. But a battery added years after solar is a perfectly normal upgrade, and for many households it is the better sequence — provided the original system was designed with that in mind.

The one number that decides it: your export profile

If you already have solar, look at how much you export during the day and what your feed-in tariff pays. When a household exports a large share of generation at a few cents per kWh while paying many times that for evening power, storage has an obvious job to do. When a household already self-consumes most of its generation because someone is home all day, the value of storage is much smaller.

If you do not have solar yet, the same logic applies in advance: estimate how much of your usage happens in daylight, and how much will be left in the evening.

When panels first is the better call

  • Your daytime usage is high — heating and cooling, pool pumps, working from home.
  • Your roof is suitable and your bill is large enough that generation has somewhere to go.
  • You want the fastest improvement in your bill for the smallest upfront commitment.
  • You are not yet sure whether you will stay in the property long enough to justify storage.

When storage first makes sense

  • You already export heavily at a low feed-in rate.
  • You have significant evening and overnight usage, often with time-of-use pricing.
  • Outage protection is a priority — a battery is the only way to keep power on.
  • You are electrifying heating, hot water or a vehicle and want to shift that load into your own generation.

Design for the battery you may add later

If a battery is likely within a few years, tell the designer now. Switchboard space, inverter choice, cable routes and the location of the battery all cost far less to plan upfront than to retrofit. You do not have to buy storage today to be ready for it.

Sizing: the mistake in both directions

Undersized storage leaves cheap self-consumption on the table. Oversized storage is capital sitting idle, particularly now that federal support tapers by capacity — the first 14 kWh of a battery attract the strongest support, and the marginal benefit falls away above 28 kWh.

A defensible starting point is to size the array to your annual consumption and the battery to your evening and overnight usage, then check the result against a year of actual data before committing.

Sequencing and incentives

Federal battery support is tied to the installation date and the program's current rules, and it is designed to work alongside solar — new or existing. State programs change more often than federal ones. If your decision is marginal, the honest advice is to model both scenarios with current prices rather than assume that waiting will produce a better outcome; support rates for both panels and batteries are generally declining over time.

Key takeaways

  • Storage value comes from the gap between a low feed-in rate and a high evening import rate.
  • Panels first suits high daytime usage; storage first suits export-heavy households with big evening loads.
  • Installing "battery-ready" costs little at the time and a lot to retrofit.
  • Federal battery support tapers by capacity, so the first kilowatt hours of storage carry the strongest support.
